questions.subject: CALCULUS_II
questions.topic: What a moment of a force records
questions.learningObjective: Explain what a moment of a force measures
questions.stem: Explain, for the logbook, what a moment of a force measures and why two equal pushes in different places can produce different turning effects.

answer.exemplar: A moment of a force measures how strongly the force tends to turn a body about a chosen pivot. It is the force multiplied by the perpendicular distance from the pivot to the line along which the force acts, so the same push applied far from the hinge turns the lid much more than the same push applied close to the hinge. What the moment records is therefore the turning effect and not the size of the force alone.

questions.explanation: A good answer defines the moment as force times perpendicular distance from the pivot and uses the hinge example. It should say the moment measures the tendency to turn rather than the force alone.
questions.hint: Say what the moment measures about turning.

questions.subject: CALCULUS_II
questions.learningObjective: Explain how a moment splits into axis components
questions.stem: Explain, in the style of the logbook, how the moment of a force about a point can be split into three components and what each component measures.

answer.exemplar: The moment of a force about a point is a vector obtained from the cross product of the position vector from the point to the point of application with the force vector. Its three components describe the turning about the x, y and z axes through that point. The z component, for instance, measures how much the force tends to spin the body about the vertical, and it is built from the horizontal forces acting at a horizontal offset, since a force along the vertical has no lever arm there. Each component therefore answers a separate question about which way the body would turn.

questions.explanation: A good answer says the moment is the cross product of position and force vectors, and that each component gives turning about one axis, built from the perpendicular force parts.
questions.hint: Each component answers about one axis.

questions.subject: CALCULUS_II
questions.learningObjective: Explain the perpendicular-axis theorem for a flat lamina
questions.stem: Explain, for the logbook, how the perpendicular-axis theorem lets you find the moment of inertia of a flat plate about an axis in its plane.

answer.exemplar: For a flat lamina lying in the xy plane, the theorem states that the moment about the z axis, perpendicular to the plate, equals the sum of the moments about the x and y axes in the plane. If the plate is symmetric, for instance a disk, the two in-plane moments are equal, so each is one half of the perpendicular value, which is one quarter of M R squared for a disk. The relation only holds for flat laminas and for axes in the same plane, and it fails for a solid body such as a sphere, where the third dimension genuinely contributes.

questions.explanation: A good answer says the perpendicular moment is the sum of the two in-plane moments for a flat lamina, and uses the symmetric disk to reach one quarter of M R squared, noting the flat-body restriction.
questions.hint: State the sum relation for a flat lamina.

questions.learningObjective: Explain why a centre of mass moves smoothly under internal shifts
questions.stem: A trolley keeps rolling smoothly even when crates are shifted inside it. Explain, in the logbook, why the centre of mass of that trolley moves smoothly under such shifts.

answer.exemplar: The centre of mass of a system is the mass-weighted average of the positions of all its parts, so shifting a crate inside the trolley moves that average by a small amount, in proportion to the crate's mass compared with the total. As long as no net external force acts along the direction of travel, the velocity of that average also stays constant, which is why the trolley carries on steadily even though its contents were disturbed.

questions.topic: What a moment of a force records
questions.learningObjective: Distinguish a moment of a force from the force itself
questions.stem: A logbook entry asks why two equal forces can produce different moments and how the moment of a force differs from the force itself.

answer.exemplar: A moment measures the turning effect of a force, so it combines how hard the force pushes with how far the push is from the pivot. Two equal forces applied at different distances from the hinge therefore give different moments, with the more distant push turning the lid more easily. The force itself is a single number in newtons, while the moment is that force multiplied by a perpendicular distance, giving newton metres, and it is the moment rather than the force that predicts how the lid will swing.

questions.explanation: A good answer distinguishes force in newtons from moment as force times perpendicular distance in newton metres, and explains that distance changes the turning effect on a lid.
questions.hint: Contrast newtons with newton metres.

answer.exemplar: A solid disk of mass M and radius R has a moment of inertia of half M R squared about the axis perpendicular to its face and only a quarter M R squared about any axis through the centre lying in its plane. The in-plane axis is the harder one to turn because the material is spread further from that axis on average, since much of the disk lies out at large radius in the plane of rotation. This is the perpendicular-axis relation at work, and it is why a wheel is far easier to spin about its axle than about a diameter.

options.misconception: believes a thin disk has no material along an in-plane axis

questions.explanation: A thin uniform disk gives a quarter of the mass times radius squared about an in-plane axis, half the perpendicular value. The hoop value does not apply to a solid disk, and thinness does not zero it.
questions.hint: Quarter of the mass times radius squared.

questions.subject: CALCULUS_II
questions.learningObjective: Derive an in-plane moment of a square plate from the theorem
questions.stem: A thin square plate in the logbook has side 0.5 metres and mass 4 kilograms. Using the perpendicular-axis theorem, give the moment of inertia about an axis in its plane through the centre, in kilogram metres squared.
questions.explanation: The perpendicular axis carries the mass times the sum of the squared sides over 12, that is 2 over 12, and the theorem splits it equally between the two in-plane axes, so each is 0.0833 kg m squared.
questions.hint: Find the perpendicular value, then halve it.

questions.subject: CALCULUS_II
questions.learningObjective: Find the volume and mass of a block in two stages
questions.stem: A block of beeswax in the logbook measures 0.3 metres by 0.2 metres by 0.1 metre and has a density of 950 kilograms per cubic metre. Find its volume and then its mass.

options.text: Volume 0.006 cubic metres and mass 5.7 kilograms, from density times volume
Volume 0.06 cubic metres and mass 57 kilograms, from a misplaced decimal point
options.misconception: misplaces the decimal and inflates both volume and mass

options.text: Volume 0.006 cubic metres and mass 0.006 kilograms, using the volume as the mass
options.misconception: reports the volume figure as though it were the mass

options.text: Volume 6 cubic metres and mass 5700 kilograms, from multiplying the edges wrongly
options.misconception: multiplies the edge lengths incorrectly to get the volume

questions.explanation: Volume is 0.3 times 0.2 times 0.1, that is 0.006 cubic metres, and mass is density times volume, giving 5.7 kg. Reporting the volume as the mass or misplacing the decimal corrupts it.
questions.hint: Find the volume first, then multiply by density.

questions.subject: CALCULUS_II
questions.topic: Motion of a centre of mass
questions.learningObjective: Picture the centre of mass as the system's effective point
questions.stem: A logbook entry states that the centre of mass of a system moves as though all the mass were concentrated at a single point. What is the most useful way to picture that statement?

options.text: As if the mass were spread evenly along the line joining the system's extremes
options.misconception: spreads the mass along the extremes rather than at one point

options.text: As if each part moved with the same speed, since the centre of mass is an average
options.misconception: reads the centre of mass as saying all parts share one speed

options.text: As if the whole mass sat at the centre of mass, for the purpose of tracking that point's motion
As if the heaviest single part of the system were moving on its own
options.misconception: confuses the centre of mass with the heaviest part's motion

questions.explanation: For tracking the motion of the centre of mass under external forces, the system behaves as though all its mass sat at that one point. It does not mean every part shares one velocity.
questions.hint: Picture all the mass at one point.
